# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Clinical and Technological Review

The transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (TV-ICD) is the cornerstone of sudden cardiac death (SCD) prevention [1]. However, transvenous leads are historically vulnerable to long-term complications, including venous thrombosis, lead fracture, tricuspid valve damage, and systemic infections [2]. To circumvent these lead-related issues, the entirely subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed [3]. By avoiding the vascular space entirely, S-ICD therapy mitigates the risks of systemic hardware infection and preserves central venous access [4].

The S-ICD system utilizes a pulse generator and a subcutaneous lead positioned left-parasternally [5]. Initially, implantations were performed using a three-incision technique, but a simplified two-incision technique has become favored to improve cosmetic outcomes, reduce procedural times, and minimize wound complications [6]. Furthermore, placing the generator in an intermuscular pocket (between the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi muscles) rather than a subcutaneous pocket has been shown to reduce post-operative pain, lower infection risks, and improve device stability [7]. The landmark PRAETORIAN trial established the clinical non-inferiority of the S-ICD compared to TV-ICDs in terms of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [8].

Despite these advantages, inappropriate shocks remain a key concern, primarily driven by T-wave oversensing (TWOS) [9]. To prevent this, patients must undergo preoperative electrocardiographic screening [10]. Specific screening tools evaluate the candidate’s QRS-to-T-wave ratio across three sensing vectors to ensure adequate signal amplitude and avoid oversensing [11]. Algorithms like the "SMART Pass" bandpass filter have significantly reduced inappropriate shocks by attenuating low-frequency signals without compromising ventricular fibrillation detection [12]. The UNTOUCHED trial demonstrated that contemporary programming and sensing algorithms reduce inappropriate shock rates to levels comparable to, or lower than, those seen with modern TV-ICDs [13].

Large-scale registries, such as the EFFORTLESS registry, have confirmed high efficacy and safety profiles in real-world clinical practice [14]. Long-term follow-up studies, including the five-year analysis of the S-ICD Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) trial, demonstrated durable performance and reliable conversion of ventricular arrhythmias [15]. When complications do occur, such as local pocket infections, the extraction of S-ICD leads is significantly less complex and carries a lower risk of catastrophic vascular damage compared to TV-ICD lead extraction [16].

Current guidelines from major professional societies support S-ICD implantation in patients without an active pacing, cardiac resynchronization, or anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) indication [17,18,19]. The device is highly recommended for young patients facing a lifelong risk of lead degradation [20], those with compromised venous access [21], and patients at high risk of system infection, such as those with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis [22]. Moreover, the S-ICD acts as a safe bridge to heart transplantation without complicating subsequent cardiac explantation or mediastinal dissection [23].

The S-ICD has also demonstrated excellent clinical utility across diverse patient populations. It is safe and effective in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) [24], congenital heart disease [25], and inherited channelopathies such as Brugada syndrome [26]. Despite the high defibrillation energy requirements historically associated with pediatric and congenital heart disease, the S-ICD has consistently demonstrated high defibrillation success in these cohorts [27].

A notable limitation of the S-ICD is its inability to deliver chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization, or ATP [28]. To address this, modular cardiac rhythm management (mCRM) systems have been developed. This approach combines the S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker (LCP), enabling wireless communication to deliver ATP or bradycardia pacing when necessary [29]. Looking ahead, future iterations focusing on longer battery life, smaller device sizes, and integrated pacing functions will likely expand the S-ICD's clinical utility [30].
